title: Cognitive Dissonance: The Engine of Self-justification
coreMove: When contradiction hurts, identify whether the person is changing behavior or merely changing the story that makes the behavior livable.
sourcePressure: This mechanism chapter explains cognitive dissonance as the pressure created when belief, behavior, and self-image collide; the source supports the smoker contradiction, Leon Festinger's failed-prophecy group, and post-choice hardening.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Reducing cognitive dissonance to ordinary discomfort or inconsistency, without showing how relief can outrun truth after commitment.

sourceAnchors.name: Leon Festinger
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports Festinger's failed-prophecy group, where a disconfirmed end-of-world expectation was reframed so commitment could survive
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Festinger's failed-prophecy group shows the trap at full heat: the world did not end, so the story had to work harder.

sourceAnchors.name: the smoker contradiction
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses a person who knows smoking is dangerous and continues smoking as the ordinary entry point for dissonance
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The smoker already has the fact; what changes is the story that lets the cigarette stay in the hand.

hook: Do not open with a generic bad habit at a kitchen table.
Avoid "everyone knows this feeling" as the first move.
counterintuition: Do not say contradiction always leads to learning.
Avoid treating certainty after commitment as proof of wisdom.
examples: No repeated smoker scenes beyond the source anchor.
No failed prophecy imitation as a fictional cult scene.

exampleSpecs.domain: a marathon trainee who keeps running on a sore tendon after buying an expensive race package
exampleSpecs.audience: readers who have invested money and identity in a plan that now hurts
exampleSpecs.stakes: a small injury could become a season-ending tear if rationalization keeps winning
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Andrew takes the printed training plan off the fridge, writes the pain score beside the nonrefundable race receipt, and decides whether the plan or the story changes
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a race receipt tucked under a blue freezer clip

exampleSpecs.domain: a school district technology committee defending a tablet purchase after teachers report low use
exampleSpecs.audience: leaders who made a public procurement choice
exampleSpecs.stakes: children lose another semester to devices nobody has integrated well
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie separates evidence that calms the committee from evidence that tests whether the tablet rollout actually helped
exampleSpecs.firstImage: thirty unopened stylus boxes stacked beside a projector cart

exampleSpecs.domain: a neighborhood restaurant owner defending a costly pizza oven that slows service
exampleSpecs.audience: small business owners attached to an expensive choice
exampleSpecs.stakes: Friday revenue keeps falling while pride turns complaints into excuses
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Etienne predicts customers will praise the new crust, then reads the ticket times aloud and marks where the defense starts replacing the evidence
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stainless peel leaning against a too-hot oven door

exampleSpecs.domain: a family investment club holding a losing clean-energy stock because selling would admit a bad call
exampleSpecs.audience: people whose judgment is publicly attached to a decision
exampleSpecs.stakes: retirement savings shrink while members search only for bullish updates
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Marta asks each member to bring one fact that would make them sell, not one fact that makes holding feel smarter
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a dividend calendar folded beside a cracked tablet case

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum membership director defending a failed exhibit theme after donors praised the concept
exampleSpecs.audience: cultural nonprofit staff balancing taste, evidence, and reputation
exampleSpecs.stakes: next season repeats the same attendance miss if praise keeps outranking foot traffic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It takes Daniel two budget meetings to see that donor compliments soothe dissonance while timed-entry data tells the harder truth
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a box of unused exhibit wristbands under the admissions desk

exampleSpecs.domain: an e-bike commuter defending a risky route because she already told friends it was the perfect switch from driving
exampleSpecs.audience: readers whose public identity is tied to a lifestyle change
exampleSpecs.stakes: near-misses accumulate while she keeps calling the route efficient
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Chiara pin a near-miss note to the route map and choose between changing streets and collecting reasons the old route is fine
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a reflective ankle band looped around a folded city bike map

skillTargets: identify dissonance reduction in a new scenario
separate evidence that relieves pressure from evidence that tests truth
evaluate when post-choice certainty signals defense rather than clarity

tryThisNowSpec: Name one choice you defended recently; write one fact that would make you revise it and one excuse that merely makes it feel better.
